solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Proud leader in the Levant?

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it, so the first piece goes inside the second

blocks.note: the Levant is the Eastern Mediterranean, shortened to E MED
a boss is the person in charge

explanation.surface: A haughty ruler somewhere in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proud' reads as arrogant, but here it means standing out from a surface. The Levant is the lands of the Eastern Mediterranean, which crosswords abbreviate to E MED.
explanation.definitionFit: Proud in the physical sense means projecting above a flat surface, which is exactly what raised, embossed lettering or decoration does.

clue.text: A gaseous element held inside mum brings forward

indicators.note: whatever is held inside something is enclosed by it, so these letters sit within the outer word

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mother
taken as written
radon is a radioactive noble gas

explanation.surface: A mother exposed to a radioactive gas somehow advances things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brings forward' looks like one verb phrase meaning to reschedule earlier; split it, and 'forward' is a noun naming a footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: Diego Maradona, the Argentine footballer, played as an attacking forward, so he is an example of a forward.

clue.text: Athletic event: come prepared with a gymslip

indicators.note: something prepared has been worked up into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl is told to turn up to sports day in her gymslip.
explanation.walkthrough: A gymslip is a sleeveless pinafore dress once worn by British schoolgirls for PE, which fits the sporty surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olympics are the world's biggest multi-sport competition, so they are an athletic event in the broad sense.

clue.text: Unhealthy group transgressed we hear — and see!

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling goes by pronunciation

blocks.note: to transgress is to sin
Rome is the seat of the Holy See, the Pope's see

explanation.surface: A sickly gang has sinned, the speaker reports, and wants you to look too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See!' reads as a command to look, but a see is a bishop's seat, and the Holy See is in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A syndrome is a set of symptoms occurring together, so it is literally a group of signs of ill health.

clue.text: One to beat clubs in bid for sports field

definitions.text: One to beat clubs in bid

blocks.clueFragment: One to beat clubs in bid
blocks.note: in bridge bidding, the suit ranked just above clubs, so one of it outbids one club
the infield of a baseball ground is this shape and takes its name

explanation.surface: Someone bids to buy a sports ground, hoping to beat the rival clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests sports clubs; it is the lowest suit in bridge bidding, and the next suit up outbids it.
explanation.definitionFit: The baseball infield, laid out as a square on its point, is universally called by this gem name, and the suit ranks second lowest.

clue.text: Soldiers struggle with critical examination

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
to vie is to compete or struggle
W is a standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Troops are having a hard time with a searching inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word joining wordplay to definition, but it supplies the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A review is a formal assessment, such as a critic's appraisal of a book or a close inspection of policy.

clue.text: Yank to succeed in forming relationship?

blocks.note: first meaning: to tug hard
second meaning: British slang for attracting someone romantically

explanation.surface: An American trying to make a romantic match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' pretends to be an American; it is the verb for jerking something. In British slang, if you pull on a night out you get off with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both tugging physically and, informally in Britain, managing to attract and pick up a romantic partner.

clue.text: Pleased with corrections accepting wit’s final column

indicators.note: corrections change what was there into something new, so the letters are reordered
the final part of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept
to accept is to take in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A newspaper humorist is happy that edits have been accepted for their column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' reads as a newspaper feature, which the surface's wit and corrections support; here it is an architectural pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base supporting a statue or pillar, and loosely a short standing column itself.

clue.text: Reserve hotel, needing flower in cool environment

blocks.note: reserve as in coolness of manner, which is also called ice
H is hotel in the NATO alphabet
a flower is something that flows, a river; the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: Booking a hotel room that must have fresh flowers in an air-conditioned setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' looks like a verb for booking; it is a noun meaning aloofness. 'Flower' is the crossword river: something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: An icehouse was a building, often partly underground, used to store ice and keep food chilled before refrigerators.

clue.text: Barnaby periodically comes to Berkshire village

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: A man called Barnaby makes regular visits to a village in Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county west of London; Bray is the village of the song 'The Vicar of Bray'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bray is a Thames-side village in Berkshire known for its celebrated restaurants and the turncoat vicar of the old song.

clue.text: Governess around isle was a wine producer

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a wine producer made Moselle, a white wine from the Moselle valley
I is an abbreviation for island or isle

explanation.surface: A former governess who once ran a vineyard on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay needs a two-word phrase: someone who was a producer of Moselle wine made Moselle.
explanation.definitionFit: In English households a French governess was traditionally addressed by the French title for an unmarried woman, so the title came to stand for the job.

clue.text: Book from town near Manchester is about a group on the rise

indicators.note: to be about something is to go round it, so one piece surrounds another
something rising goes upward, which in a down entry turns the letters back to front

blocks.note: Eccles is a town just west of Manchester, known for its currant cakes
taken as written
taken as written
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A book set in a Lancashire town about a band whose fame is growing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' could be any volume; here it is a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecclesiastes is one of the wisdom books of the Old Testament, famous for 'vanity of vanities'.

clue.text: Sweetheart knocked back vermouth in second cocktail

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the letters run the other way
one thing in another is enclosed by it, so the pair goes inside

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
jo is a Scots word for a sweetheart, as in Burns's 'John Anderson, my jo'
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: A lover downs a vermouth, then quickly moves on to a second drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' reads as drinking, but it reverses the sweetheart; 'second' is not a second cocktail but a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A mojito is a Cuban highball of white rum, lime, sugar, mint and soda water, so it is one kind of mixed drink.

clue.text: Show the four holding hands with model

blocks.note: the four bridge players, each holding a hand of cards, sit North, East, West and South
to cast is to shape in a mould, to model

explanation.surface: A performance where the quartet link hands with a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding hands' paints affection, but the hands are cards at the bridge table, where the four players are named for compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: A newscast is a broadcast programme of the news, so it is a kind of television or radio show.

clue.text: Landmass created by Greek god and goddess

blocks.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild and shepherds
Gaea, or Gaia, is the Greek goddess of the Earth

explanation.surface: A myth in which a continent was made by a pair of Greek deities.
explanation.walkthrough: The goddess needs the less common spelling Gaea rather than Gaia.
explanation.definitionFit: Pangaea was the single supercontinent that existed before continental drift split it into today's continents.

clue.text: Crow after lemonade, then home for macaroni?

indicators.note: coming after something means placed later in the line, fixing which part comes last

blocks.note: pop is fizzy drink such as lemonade
to be in is to be at home
the jay is a member of the crow family

explanation.surface: A meal plan: a bird, a fizzy drink, then back home for pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Macaroni' looks like pasta; the question mark flags its old sense of an 18th-century dandy in extravagant continental fashions.
explanation.definitionFit: A popinjay is a vain, showily dressed man, just what an 18th-century macaroni was: a foppish follower of fashion.

clue.text: Always in drawing room, going away different

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it, so the first piece goes inside
something sent away is no longer there, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: a salon is an elegant reception room
ever means always
a machine that is going is on

explanation.surface: Someone always leaves the drawing room looking changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going away' reads as one phrase for leaving; split it, 'going' means working, and 'away' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Several can mean separate or distinct, as in 'they went their several ways', so it matches different.

clue.text: Former partner went to collect learners sent down

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
to go, informally, is to urinate
L is learner, as on a learner driver's plate; two of them

explanation.surface: An ex went to pick up some learner drivers who had been sent away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' has a coarse sense: to go is to relieve oneself. 'Sent down' is British university slang for being thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: A student sent down has been dismissed from a British university, which is to be thrown out of the institution.

clue.text: Defence of Post Office record one’s put in two answers

indicators.note: what is put in something ends up inside it, so these pieces go within the outer letters

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer; two of them
PO is the abbreviation
a log is a written record
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Post Office defends itself by entering its records into a pair of replies.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the Post Office scandal in Britain, where false records led to wrongful prosecutions; 'Defence' is not a legal plea here but a written justification.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologia is a formal written defence of one's opinions or conduct, like Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua.

clue.text: Outdated proposal of law used for the Met?

blocks.note: outdated things are old
a bill is a proposed law put before parliament

explanation.surface: An obsolete piece of legislation once applied to the Metropolitan Police.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met is London's Metropolitan Police; 'the Old Bill' is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is everyday British slang for the police in general and London's Metropolitan force in particular.

clue.text: Earliest vampire bats seen by lake

indicators.note: someone bats is crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: The first vampire bats were spotted near a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vampire bats' looks like a single animal name; 'bats' is the signal to rearrange 'vampire'.
explanation.definitionFit: Primeval describes the very first ages of the world, the most ancient and original times.

clue.text: One causing damage in V&A close to fanatical

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is used

blocks.note: the ampersand is read out as the word 'and'
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fanatic nearly causing harm inside the Victoria and Albert Museum.
explanation.walkthrough: The V&A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, fitting the surface of a gallery attack.
explanation.definitionFit: A vandal is someone who deliberately destroys or defaces property, which is exactly a person causing damage.

clue.text: French fish giving up a small something found in fugu?

indicators.note: to give something up is to let it go, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: poisson is the French word for fish
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A French fish that has lost a bit of its size turns up in a Japanese dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Fugu is Japanese pufferfish, a delicacy that must be expertly prepared because parts of it are deadly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fugu organs hold tetrodotoxin, a lethal toxin, so the deadly substance is what diners risk finding in it.

clue.text: Basic facts: Bond in tussle with sultan before thugs cleared out

indicators.note: things in a tussle are thrown about and jumbled, so the letters are mixed up
a room cleared out has nothing left in the middle, so only its outer letters remain
coming before something means placed earlier in the line, setting the order of the parts

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: James Bond grapples with a sultan before his henchmen are cleared away, as in a spy film.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond and the sultan are not characters here, just letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for the essential practical details of a subject, the fundamentals everything else rests on.

clue.text: Extremely good but never quiet: is that Gobbi?

definitions.note: a first name: the definition asks for the forename of the singer

indicators.note: what never appears is absent, so every instance of the letter is removed

blocks.note: tiptop means excellent
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: An opera fan asks whether a superb but always loud singer is Gobbi.
explanation.walkthrough: Tito Gobbi was a celebrated Italian operatic baritone of the mid-20th century. Both copies of the quiet letter go.
explanation.definitionFit: Tito was the given name of Gobbi, the Italian baritone famous for Scarpia in Tosca, so that Gobbi is Tito.

clue.text: Marked for deportation in African country?

blocks.note: first meaning: someone marked for removal is due to be sent away
second meaning: the small West African republic

explanation.walkthrough: The solution's letters are both a two-word phrase for 'due to leave' and the name of a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A person earmarked for expulsion is one who has to leave, and Togo is a West African nation between Ghana and Benin.

clue.text: Ace business publication with energy slowing in the end

blocks.note: A is ace in cards
the FT is the Financial Times
E is the physics symbol for energy
rall. is short for rallentando, the musical direction to slow down

explanation.surface: A top financial paper finally runs out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slowing' needs the musical abbreviation rall., from rallentando.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean eventually or when everything is considered, so they swap in a sentence like 'it rained after all'.

clue.text: Guide southern sailor following sound of albatross?

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is spoken, so the spelling follows pronunciation
what follows comes later in line, fixing which part is placed second

blocks.note: an albatross round one's neck is a burden, from Coleridge's Ancient Mariner
S is southern
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A seafarer navigating the southern oceans by the cry of an albatross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Albatross' is not the bird but a burden, after the dead albatross the Ancient Mariner had to wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodestar is a star used to steer by, especially the Pole Star, and figuratively any guiding principle.
